title.rhyme: Chapter 3: Dong Zhuo, in Wenming's hall, Ding Yuan berates; Li Su, with gold and pearl, Lü Bu persuades.
title.prose: Chapter 3: At the Wenming council, Dong Zhuo berates Ding Yuan; with gifts of gold and pearl, Li Su persuades Lü Bu.
title.original: 第三回：議溫明董卓叱丁原，餽金珠李肅說呂布

paragraphs.original: 且說曹操當日對何進曰：「宦官之禍，古今皆有；但世主不當假之權寵，使至於此。若欲治罪，當除元惡，但付一獄吏足矣，何必紛紛召外兵乎？欲盡誅之，事必宣露。吾料其必敗也。」何進怒曰：「孟德亦懷私意耶？」操退曰：「亂天下者，必進也。」進乃暗差使命齎密詔，星夜往各鎮去。
paragraphs.prose: Now to tell of Cao Cao, who that day spoke before He Jin, saying: "The evil of the eunuchs is found in every age, ancient and present; but only when the rulers of the world have wrongly entrusted them with power and favor have they come to such a pass. If you would punish their crimes, you should cut off only the chief offenders; one jail-officer would suffice — what need to summon outside troops in confusion? If you would put them all to death, the matter must be made public; I reckon the design will surely fail." He Jin angrily answered, "Does Mengde too harbor a private mind?" Cao Cao withdrew, saying, "He who shall bring chaos upon the empire — it shall be Jin." He Jin then secretly dispatched envoys, bearing sealed edicts, by night, to each frontier garrison.
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) to [He Jin](char-he-jin) spake that very day:
"The eunuchs' woe is ancient — yet the way
That rulers vested them with pow'r and grace,
Hath brought our state, by stages, to disgrace.
To punish wrongs, cut off the chiefest head:
One jailer's hand shall lay the guilty dead.
What need to summon outer troops, in throng?
The plot, once spread, must surely come out wrong.
I look — and see the failure of thy plan."
[He Jin](char-he-jin), enrag'd: "Doth [Mengde](char-cao-cao), like these, scan
With private mind?" [Cao](char-cao-cao) made reply, withdrew:
"'Tis [Jin](char-he-jin) himself, who shall the realm undo."
[He Jin](char-he-jin), in secret, by the dead of night,
Sent seal'd decrees to garrisons in flight.

paragraphs.original: 卻說前將軍鰲鄉侯西涼刺史董卓，先為破黃巾無功，朝廷將治其罪，因賄賂十常侍幸免；後又結託朝貴，遂任顯官，統西州大軍二十萬，常有不臣之心。是時得詔大喜，點起軍馬，陸續便行；使其婿中郎將牛輔，守住陝西，自己卻帶李傕、郭汜、張濟、樊稠等提兵望洛陽進發。卓婿謀士李儒曰：「今雖奉詔，中間多有暗昧。何不差人上表，名正言順，大事可圖。」卓大喜，遂上表。其略曰：　　竊聞天下所以亂逆不止者，皆由黃門常侍張讓等侮慢天常之故。臣聞揚湯止沸，不如去薪；潰癰雖痛，勝於養毒。臣敢鳴鐘鼓入洛陽，請除讓等。社稷幸甚！天下幸甚！
paragraphs.prose: Now to tell of the General of the Front, Marquis of Aoxiang, and Inspector of Xiliang Dong Zhuo. He had earlier proved without merit in breaking the Yellow Turbans, and the court was about to punish him; but by bribes to the Ten Permanent Attendants he was pardoned, and afterwards bound himself to the great men at court, and so was raised to a prominent office, having command of two hundred thousand troops of the western region — and yet he had ever in his heart a mind unsubmissive to his sovereign. At this time, receiving the edict, he was greatly pleased, and at once mustered his troops and horses, and set them in motion in succession. He appointed his son-in-law, the General of the Household Niu Fu, to hold Shaanxi, and himself led Li Jue, Guo Si, Zhang Ji, and Fan Chou, marching with their troops toward Luoyang. His son-in-law and strategist Li Ru said, "Although Your Lordship now bears the edict, there are many shadowed things within. Why not send a man with a memorial, that the name be just and the words proper — and the great matter may be encompassed?" Dong Zhuo was greatly pleased, and at once sent up the memorial. Its substance ran: "I have heard that the reason the empire's rebellions and disorders have not been stopped is because of Zhang Rang and the rest, the Yellow Gate Permanent Attendants, who slight and disregard the constant law of Heaven. Your servant has heard: 'To bail the boiling water and so still it is not as good as taking out the firewood; to lance an abscess, though painful, is better than feeding the poison.' Your servant therefore ventures to sound the bells and drums and to enter Luoyang, asking to remove Zhang Rang and the rest. Fortunate is the state! Fortunate is the realm!"
paragraphs.rhyme:
Of [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) now: Front General held command,
Aoxiang's Marquis, chief of [Xiliang](loc-xiliang)'s land;
'Gainst Yellow Turbans first no merit won,
The court would judge him; but his bribes had run
To those Ten Servants, and he 'scap'd that day.
Then, knit with courtly lords, he found a way
To high command — with troops of western land,
Two hundred thousand under his right hand;
And ever held a heart to treason prone.
Receiving now the edict, joy was sown;
He muster'd horse and foot in marching line.
Niu Fu, his son-in-law, by court's design,
Was bid to hold Shaanxi; while [Dong](char-dong-zhuo) led on
[Li Jue](char-li-jue), [Guo Si](char-guo-si), [Zhang Ji](char-zhang-ji), [Fan Chou](char-fan-chou) — anon
Toward [Luoyang](loc-luoyang) his host in order flew,
Through plain and pass, the army's track they drew.
[Li Ru](char-li-ru), his son-in-law, spoke in this guise:
"Though by decree we march, much shadow lies;
Send first a memorial on the road,
That name and words may bear a proper load.
Then shall the great affair have lawful air."
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) heard, and took the counsel there,
And straight a memorial to the throne he sent.
Its substance: "I have heard the realm's woe-rent
Springs from [Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang), the [Yellow Gate](misc-yellow-gate)'s foul crew,
Whose slights upon Heaven's law are nothing new.
'Tis said: To still the boiling pot, the way
Is to remove the kindling — not to spray
Cool water; lance the boil doth pain, but worse
Is feeding poison's growth, the body's curse.
I dare with bells and drums to [Luoyang](loc-luoyang) go,
To purge [Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang) and the [Yellow Gate](misc-yellow-gate) foe;
How fortunate the state and realm shall grow!"

paragraphs.original: 何進得表，出示大臣。侍御史鄭泰諫曰：「董卓乃豺狼也，引入京城，必食人矣。」進曰：「汝多疑，不足謀大事。」盧植亦諫曰：「植素知董卓為人，面善心狠；一入禁庭，必生禍患。不如止之勿來，免致生亂。」
paragraphs.prose: He Jin received the memorial and showed it to the great ministers. The Imperial Censor Zheng Tai remonstrated, saying, "Dong Zhuo is a wolf and a jackal; bring him into the capital, and he will surely devour men." He Jin said, "You are too full of suspicion, and not fit to plan great matters." Lu Zhi too remonstrated, saying, "I have long known the nature of Dong Zhuo: gentle of countenance, cruel of heart; once let into the inner palace, he will breed calamity. Better to stay him from coming, that disorder be averted."
paragraphs.rhyme:
[He Jin](char-he-jin) receiv'd the writ, and show'd it wide.
Zheng Tai, the Censor, rose, his words to chide:
"[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) is wolf and jackal — should we call,
He'd eat the men of court within our hall."
[He Jin](char-he-jin) reply'd in scorn: "Thy doubts are vain,
Such fearful heart no great affair shall gain."
[Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi) too counsell'd: "Long have I divin'd
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s true face: smooth visage, cruel mind;
Once let him enter, mischief shall be born;
Far better stay him, ere our peace be torn."

paragraphs.original: 進不聽，鄭泰、盧植皆棄官而去。朝廷大臣，去者大半。進使人迎董卓於澠池，卓按兵不動。張讓等知外兵到，共議曰：「此何進之謀也；我等不先下手，皆滅族矣。」乃先伏刀斧手五十人於長樂宮嘉德門內，入告何太后曰：「今大將軍矯詔召外兵至京師，欲滅臣等，望娘娘垂憐賜救。」太后曰：「汝等可詣大將軍府謝罪。」讓曰：「若到相府，骨肉虀粉矣。望娘娘宣大將軍入宮諭止之。如其不從，臣等只就娘娘前請死。」
paragraphs.prose: He Jin gave no heed; Zheng Tai and Lu Zhi both relinquished their offices and departed; of the great ministers of the court, more than half went also. He Jin sent men to welcome Dong Zhuo at Mianchi; but Zhuo held his troops in check, and would not advance. Zhang Rang and the rest, learning that the outer forces had come, took counsel together: "This is the plot of He Jin; if we do not strike first, our clans will be utterly destroyed." So they hid fifty men with swords and axes within the Jiade Gate of the Changle Palace, and went in to inform the Empress Dowager He, saying, "Now the Grand General has, by a forged edict, summoned outer troops to the capital, intending to destroy us your servants — we beseech Your Majesty's pity and rescue." The Empress Dowager said, "You may go to the Grand General's office and apologize." Rang said, "If we go to his Lordship's residence, our flesh and bones shall be ground to powder. We beg Your Majesty to summon the Grand General into the palace and bid him desist; should he not consent, your servants shall die in Your Majesty's presence."
paragraphs.rhyme:
[He Jin](char-he-jin) would heed not; Zheng Tai turn'd away,
With [Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi) — both resign'd, in deep dismay.
Half of the court's great lords forsook their place;
[He Jin](char-he-jin) sent men to greet, with friendly grace,
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) at Mianchi. There [Dong](char-dong-zhuo) held his band,
And march'd no further: still upon the land.
[Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang) and his, who heard that outer arms
Had come, took counsel: "This bears [Jin](char-he-jin)'s alarms;
Strike we not first, our clans shall fall undone."
Then fifty axemen in concealment, on
The Jiade Gate of Changle, were they hid.
To [Empress He](char-empress-he) they came, and pleading slid:
"The Grand General, by edict feign'd, hath call'd
Outside-bound troops, to crush us thus enthrall'd.
Have pity, sovereign! Save thy servants now!"
The [Empress](char-empress-he) said: "Then go to him, and bow."
[Rang](char-zhang-rang) answer'd: "Were we sent unto his door,
Our flesh and bones to powder shall be tore.
Pray bid him to the palace; should he stay,
Before thy throne we'll die without delay."

paragraphs.original: 太后乃降詔宣進。進得詔便行。主簿陳琳諫曰：「太后此詔，必是十常侍之謀，切不可去。去必有禍。」進曰：「太后詔我，有何禍事？」袁紹曰：「今謀已泄，事已露，將軍尚欲入宮耶？」曹操曰：「先召十常侍出，然後可入。」進笑曰：「此小兒之見也。吾掌天下之權，十常侍敢待如何？」紹曰：「公必欲去，我等引甲士護從，以防不測。」
paragraphs.prose: The Empress Dowager then sent down an edict summoning He Jin. He Jin, on receiving the edict, set out at once. The Chief Recorder Chen Lin remonstrated, saying, "This edict from the Empress must be the design of the Ten Permanent Attendants; do not go on any account — to go is to incur calamity." He Jin said, "The Empress summons me herself; what calamity is there?" Yuan Shao said, "Now that the design is leaked and the matter known, would Your Lordship still enter the palace?" Cao Cao said, "Summon out the Ten Permanent Attendants first, then you may enter." He Jin laughed, "This is the view of a little child! I hold the power of the empire — what dare the Ten Permanent Attendants do to me?" Shao said, "If My Lord must go, we will lead armed escort to safeguard against the unforeseen."
paragraphs.rhyme:
The [Empress](char-empress-he) sent her summons — [Jin](char-he-jin) obey'd,
And rose to go. Chen Lin, alarm'd, then said:
"This edict from the queen the Ten have plann'd;
Go not, my lord — great peril is at hand."
[He Jin](char-he-jin) reply'd: "The [Empress](char-empress-he) calls me here,
What danger doth her summons bring me near?"
[Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) now spake: "The plot is leak'd, the foe
Forewarn'd: shouldst thou unto the palace go?"
[Cao Cao](char-cao-cao): "First call the Ten Attendants out;
Then thou mayst enter, freed of all their doubt."
[He Jin](char-he-jin) laugh'd loud: "A childish view, enow!
I hold the empire's power — none my brow
Shall vex." Said [Shao](char-yuan-shao): "If go thou must, attend
We will, with arm'd escort, all harm to fend."

paragraphs.original: 於是袁紹、曹操各選精兵五百，命袁紹之弟袁術領之。袁術全身披掛，引兵布列青瑣門外。紹與操帶劍護送何進至長樂宮前。黃門傳懿旨云：「太后特宣大將軍，餘人不許輒入。」將袁紹、曹操等都阻住宮門外。何進昂然直入。至嘉德殿門，張讓、段珪迎出，左右圍住，進大驚。讓厲聲責進曰：「董后何罪，妄以酖死？國母喪葬，託疾不出！汝本屠沽小輩，我等薦之天子，以致榮貴：不思報效，欲相謀害！汝言我等甚濁，其清者是誰？」進慌急，欲尋出路，宮門盡閉，伏甲齊出，將何進砍為兩段。後人有詩歎之曰：漢室傾危天數終，無謀何進作三公。幾番不聽忠臣諫，難免宮中受劍鋒。
paragraphs.prose: Thereupon Yuan Shao and Cao Cao each chose five hundred picked troops, and gave them to Yuan Shao's younger brother Yuan Shu to command. Yuan Shu, in full armor, drew up the troops in array outside the Qingsuo Gate. Shao and Cao, with swords drawn, escorted He Jin to the front of the Changle Palace. A Yellow Gate transmitted the imperial command, saying, "The Empress Dowager especially summons the Grand General; the rest may not enter on any account." Yuan Shao, Cao Cao, and the others were therefore blocked outside the palace gate. He Jin, with bold mien, entered straight in. At the door of the Jiade Hall, Zhang Rang and Duan Gui came forth to meet him; left and right, others ringed him round, and He Jin was greatly startled. Rang, with stern voice, rebuked He Jin, saying: "What crime had Empress Dowager Dong, that thou shouldst causelessly poison her to death? When the State Mother was being mourned and buried, thou didst feign illness and not come forth! Thou art but a paltry fellow of butchers and wine-sellers; it was we who recommended thee to the Son of Heaven, that thou mightest enjoy honor and wealth — thou hast not thought to repay our kindness, but seekest to compass our murder! Thou sayest that we are foul — and who, then, is the pure?" He Jin, in panic and confusion, sought a way out; but the palace gates were all closed, and the men in concealment, fully armored, came forth at once and hacked He Jin into two pieces. A later poet sighed of him in verse, saying: "The Han house tottered, Heaven's count was done; / He Jin, without design, was made a minister. / Many times he hearkened not to loyal counsel — / Hard could he 'scape the sword-edge in the palace."
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) and [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) each chose five hundred bold;
[Yuan Shu](char-yuan-shu) the younger brother was enroll'd
In leadership; full-arm'd, he led the band
Without the Qingsuo Gate in martial stand.
With swords, [Shao](char-yuan-shao) and [Cao](char-cao-cao) escorted [Jin](char-he-jin)
Up to the Changle Palace gate within.
A [Yellow Gate](misc-yellow-gate) then bade the call repeat:
"The [Empress](char-empress-he) wills the General to her seat;
The rest abide without — none shall pass o'er."
So [Shao](char-yuan-shao), [Cao](char-cao-cao), and others held the door.
[He Jin](char-he-jin), with bold demeanor, enter'd plain.
Before the Jiade Hall, two foes maintain'd
Their watch: [Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang) and [Duan Gui](char-duan-gui) — left and right
They circled him; [He Jin](char-he-jin), in sudden fright,
Stood pale. [Rang](char-zhang-rang) loudly chid: "What crime had [Dong](char-empress-dowager-dong),
That thou with poison slew? At her grand funeral, long
Thou stay'dst at home. A butcher's mean brood thou,
We rais'd thee up before the throne; allow'd
Thy rise to wealth and rank: thou hast not paid
With gratitude, but for our blood hast pray'd!
Thou call'st us foul — yet in thy pride explain
Who is the pure one." — [Jin](char-he-jin), in panic plain,
Sought exit; all the gates fast lock'd were found,
The hidden armed men sprang from out the ground,
And hacked [He Jin](char-he-jin) in two beside the hall.
A later poet sighed; these lines let fall:
"The Han house tilts; the count of heaven done;
[He Jin](char-he-jin), no plan, the Three Excellencies' won;
Times oft he hark'd not honest minister's word,
Hard 'twas to 'scape the palace blade's keen sword."

paragraphs.original: 讓等既殺何進，袁紹久不見進出，乃於宮門外大叫曰：「請將軍上車！」讓等將何進首級從牆上擲出，宣諭曰：「何進謀反，已伏誅矣。其餘脅從，盡皆赦宥。」袁紹厲聲大叫：「閹官謀殺大臣！誅惡黨者前來助戰！」何進部將吳匡，便於青瑣門外放起火來。袁術引兵突入宮庭，但見閹官，不諭大小，盡皆殺之。袁紹、曹操斬關入內。趙忠，程曠，夏惲，郭勝四個被趕至翠花樓前，剁為肉泥。宮中火燄沖天。張讓，段珪，曹節，侯覽將太后及太子并陳留王劫去內省，從後道走北宮。
paragraphs.prose: Now Rang and the rest, having slain He Jin, Yuan Shao for a long while did not see him come out. He stood at the palace gate and shouted aloud, "Please, General, mount your carriage!" Rang and his fellows threw He Jin's head from the wall, and proclaimed, "He Jin plotted treason and has already been executed; all the rest who were forced into his ways are pardoned without exception." Yuan Shao with a great voice cried out, "The eunuchs have murdered a great minister! Let those who would put the evil party to death come forward and aid in the fight!" He Jin's general Wu Kuang at once set fire outside the Qingsuo Gate. Yuan Shu led his troops in a sudden rush into the palace courts, and slew every eunuch he saw, regardless of high or low. Shao and Cao broke through the gates, and entered. Zhao Zhong, Cheng Kuang, Xia Yun, and Guo Sheng — four men — were driven before the Cuihua Tower, and there hacked into pulp. The flames in the palace shot up to heaven. Zhang Rang, Duan Gui, Cao Jie, and Hou Lan seized the Empress, the Crown Prince, and the Prince of Chenliu, and forced them away through the inner palace, fleeing by the back path toward the North Palace.
paragraphs.rhyme:
When [Rang](char-zhang-rang) had slain [Jin](char-he-jin), [Shao](char-yuan-shao) kept watch below;
Long time he saw him not, and cried out so:
"Pray, General, mount thy car and come!"
The answer from the wall struck all men dumb:
[Rang](char-zhang-rang) and his fellows cast [He Jin](char-he-jin)'s severed head,
And cried aloud the charge their malice spread:
"[He Jin](char-he-jin) plotted treason; judgment struck him dead;
The rest were forced to follow where he led.
All such are pardoned; none the stroke shall bear."
Then [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) thundered forth with wrathful air,
Cried back: "The eunuchs have a minister slain!
Who would the evil party slay, advance amain!"
Wu Kuang, the General's man, before the gate
Of Qingsuo, lit the flames of furious hate.
[Yuan Shu](char-yuan-shu) with troops the palace courts broke in,
And kill'd each eunuch — high or low, no kin
Was spar'd. With swords [Shao](char-yuan-shao), [Cao](char-cao-cao) smash'd the door.
[Zhao Zhong](char-zhao-zhong), [Cheng Kuang](char-cheng-kuang), [Xia Yun](char-xia-yun), [Guo Sheng](char-guo-sheng) — these four
Were driv'n to Cuihua's tow'r and there hew'd small,
To mincemeat hack'd. The flames of palace-hall
Did mount to heaven. [Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang), with [Duan Gui](char-duan-gui),
[Cao Jie](char-cao-jie), and [Hou Lan](char-hou-lan) — four — in flight made way,
They snatch'd the [Empress](char-empress-he), [Crown Prince](char-prince-bian), [Chenliu](char-prince-xie) too,
And by back-paths to the North Palace flew.

paragraphs.original: 時盧植棄官未去，見宮中事變，擐甲持戈，立於閣下。遙見段珪擁逼何后過來，植大呼曰：「段珪逆賊，安敢劫太后！」段珪回身便走。太后從窗中跳出，植急救得免。吳匡殺入內庭，見何苗亦提劍出。匡大呼曰：「何苗同謀害兄，當共殺之！」眾人俱曰：「願斬謀兄之賊！」苗欲走，四面圍定，砍為虀粉。紹復令軍士分頭來殺十常侍家屬，不分大小，盡皆誅絕，多有無鬚者誤被殺死。曹操一面救滅宮中之火，請何太后權攝大事，遣兵追襲張讓等，尋覓少帝。
paragraphs.prose: At that time Lu Zhi, who had given up his office but had not yet departed, seeing what was happening in the palace, donned his armor and grasped his spear, and stood beneath the hall. From a distance he saw Duan Gui forcing Empress He to come out. Lu Zhi cried with a loud voice, "Duan Gui, traitor and rebel — how darest thou seize the Empress!" Duan Gui turned and fled. The Empress leapt from a window; Lu Zhi was just in time to save her. Wu Kuang charged into the inner court, and saw He Miao also drawing his sword and coming forth. Kuang cried out, "He Miao plotted to do his brother to death — let us together slay him!" All the men shouted, "We will slay the betrayer of his brother!" Miao tried to flee, but they ringed him about on all four sides, and hacked him into pulp. Shao then ordered his soldiers to divide and go forth to slay all the kindred of the Ten Permanent Attendants — regardless of high or low, every one of them was put to death; and many beardless men were thus mistakenly slain. Cao Cao, on his side, extinguished the fires within the palace, and asked Empress Dowager He to take charge of affairs in the meantime; he then dispatched troops to pursue Zhang Rang and the rest, and to seek the young Emperor.
paragraphs.rhyme:
Now [Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi), who had quit his office but
Had not yet gone, beheld the palace shut
With strife. He arm'd himself with mail and lance,
And stood beneath the hall, with watchful glance.
He saw, far off, [Duan Gui](char-duan-gui) in headlong flight,
The [Empress He](char-empress-he) with him compell'd by might.
[Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi) cried out: "[Duan Gui](char-duan-gui), thou rebel-knave!
How darest thou the [Empress](char-empress-he) thus enslave?"
Duan turn'd and fled. The [Empress](char-empress-he), in her fear,
Sprang from a window — [Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi) caught her near.
Wu Kuang, in fury, broke into the court,
Saw [He Miao](char-he-miao) with drawn sword, in mute resort.
Wu Kuang cried loud: "[He Miao](char-he-miao) his brother sold —
Together strike him down, my comrades bold!"
All shouted: "Slay the brother-betrayer here!"
[Miao](char-he-miao) would have fled, but ringed about by spear,
Was hack'd to pieces. [Shao](char-yuan-shao) then bade his men
Divide their force, and slay the eunuch kin,
Regardless of degree, all to be slain;
And many beardless men were kill'd in vain.
[Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) the palace fires put out with care,
Then bade the [Empress He](char-empress-he) the regent's chair
To fill, while troops were sent the foe to chase,
And seek the lost young Emp'ror's piteous case.

paragraphs.original: 且說張讓，段珪，劫擁少帝及陳留王，冒煙突火，連夜奔走至北邙山。約三更時分，後面喊聲大舉，人馬趕至；當前何南中部掾吏閔貢，大呼：「逆賊休走！」張讓見事急，遂投河而死。帝與陳留王未知虛實，不敢高聲，伏於河邊亂草之內。軍馬四散去趕，不知帝之所在。
paragraphs.prose: Now to tell of Zhang Rang and Duan Gui, who, having seized the young Emperor and the Prince of Chenliu, braved smoke and fire and fled by night until they came to Mount Beimang. About the third watch a great clamor arose behind them, and men and horses came up. From the front the He'nan Bureau Officer Min Gong gave a loud cry, "Rebel thieves, halt!" Zhang Rang, seeing the matter desperate, cast himself into the river and was drowned. The Emperor and the Prince of Chenliu, not knowing how things stood, dared not raise their voices, and lay hidden in the rank grass beside the river. The horsemen scattered in pursuit, and knew not where the Emperor was.
paragraphs.rhyme:
Now [Rang](char-zhang-rang) and Gui, who seiz'd the King and heir
Of [Chenliu](char-prince-xie), through smoke and flame did fare
Their flight, by night, to Beimang's lonely mount.
About third watch, behind, a great account
Of cries arose; men, horses, in pursuit
Came on. Before, Min Gong, with stern repute,
Of He'nan, cried in voice of bold command:
"Halt, rebel-thieves!" — Min Gong was right at hand.
[Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang) perceived the crisis drawing near,
And drowned himself within the waters clear.
The Emp'ror and the Prince knew not the case;
Dar'd not their voices raise; nor stir from grass.
Horsemen scour'd far, by ev'ry path and way,
Yet found not where the boy-King hidden lay.

paragraphs.original: 帝與王伏至四更，露水又下，腹中飢餒，相抱而哭；又怕人知覺，吞聲草莽之中。陳留王曰：「此間不可久戀，須別尋活路。」於是二人以衣相結，爬上岸邊。滿地荊棘，黑暗之中，不見行路。正無奈何，忽有流螢千百成群，光芒照耀，只在帝前飛轉。陳留王曰：「此天助我兄弟也！」遂隨螢火而行，漸漸見路。行至五更，足痛不能行。山岡邊見一草堆，帝與王臥於草堆之畔。草堆前面是一所莊院。莊主是夜夢兩紅日墜於莊後，驚覺，披衣出戶，四下觀望。見莊後草堆上紅光沖天，慌忙往視，卻是二人臥於草畔。
paragraphs.prose: The Emperor and the Prince lay hidden until the fourth watch; the dew was falling, and they were hungry, and embraced each other and wept; yet, fearing they should be discovered, they swallowed their voices in the grass. The Prince of Chenliu said, "We cannot remain long here; we must seek another way to live." Then the two of them tied their clothes together, and climbed up to the bank. The ground was full of brambles, and in the darkness they could not see the path. While they were at their wits' end, suddenly there came a thousand fireflies in a flock, with shining lights, that flew round and round in front of the Emperor alone. The Prince of Chenliu said, "This is heaven's help to us brothers!" Then they followed the firefly-light onward, and gradually came in sight of a path. They walked till the fifth watch; their feet ached, and they could go no further. Beside the hill they saw a heap of grass, and the Emperor and the Prince lay down beside the grass-heap. In front of the grass-heap was a manor-house. The lord of the manor that night dreamed that two red suns had fallen behind his manor; he was startled awake, threw on his clothes, and came out to look about him. He saw a red light, shooting up to heaven from the grass-heap behind his manor, and hurriedly went to look — and there he found two persons lying beside the grass.
paragraphs.rhyme:
Until the fourth watch, hidden lay the two,
Dew falling cold; they hungered through and through.
They lock'd their arms in tears, but, fearing ear,
They stifled sound in grass — a piteous fear.
The [Chenliu Prince](char-prince-xie) spake out: "We cannot stay
In this poor cover; let us seek a way."
The two their garments knotted; up the bank
They climb'd, where bramble in the darkness sank
The path beyond their sight. As wits' end fell,
A thousand glow-flies came in shining spell;
A swarm before the Emp'ror wheeled and played,
Their glow revealing where the path was laid.
The [Prince](char-prince-xie) cried: "Heaven aids us — be of cheer!"
Then by the firefly-light, with way grown clear,
They onward hied. They walk'd till fifth-watch hour;
Their feet now ach'd, no further could endure.
Beside a hill, a heap of grass they saw;
And by it, both lay down beneath its straw.
A manor stood near by; the manor-head
That night had dream'd of two red suns, that sped
Behind his house. He leapt awake, in fear,
Threw on his robe, came forth, and look'd anear.
He saw a crimson light from heaven shed,
Rise from the grass-heap of his manor-stead.
He hasten'd to inspect, with quick'ning pace;
There found two persons in the grass-heap's space.

paragraphs.original: 莊主問曰：「二少年誰家之子？」帝不敢應。陳留王指帝曰：「此是當今皇帝，遭十常侍之亂，逃難到此。吾乃皇弟陳留王也。」莊主大驚，再拜曰：「臣先朝司徒崔烈之弟崔毅也。因見十常侍賣官嫉賢，故隱於此。」遂扶帝入莊，跪進酒食。
paragraphs.prose: The manor-lord asked, "Of what house are these two young men?" The Emperor dared not answer. The Prince of Chenliu, pointing to the Emperor, said, "This is the present Emperor, who has suffered the disorder of the Ten Permanent Attendants and fled hither in distress. I am his younger brother, the Prince of Chenliu." The manor-lord was greatly startled, and bowing twice, said, "Your servant is Cui Yi, the younger brother of the former Minister of the Masses Cui Lie. Because I saw the Ten Permanent Attendants selling office and hating men of worth, I withdrew and hid myself here." He thereupon helped the Emperor into the manor, and kneeling, offered wine and food.
paragraphs.rhyme:
The manor-lord enquir'd: "Whose sons are ye?"
The Emp'ror durst not answer, fearfully.
The [Prince of Chenliu](char-prince-xie) pointed: "This is he,
Our Emp'ror, who hath fled the Ten's decree
Of chaos. I his brother, Chenliu's royal head."
The host, much startled, twice bow'd low, and said:
"I, Cui Yi, brother of the Excellence
Cui Lie, who fled the court's foul pestilence,
The Ten sold office, scorning men of grace;
I hid myself within this lonely place."
He led them in, and bow'd in courteous wise,
And serv'd them wine and food before their eyes.

paragraphs.original: 卻說閔貢趕上段珪拏住，問天子何在。珪言已在半路相失，不知何往。貢遂殺段珪，懸頭於馬項下，分兵四散尋覓；自己卻獨乘一馬，隨路追尋。偶至崔毅莊，毅見首級，問之，貢說詳細。崔毅引貢見帝，君臣痛哭。貢曰：「國不可一日無君，請陛下還都。」崔毅莊上只有瘦馬一匹，備與帝乘。貢與陳留王共乘一馬。離莊而行，不到三里，司徒王允，太尉楊彪，左軍校尉淳于瓊，右軍校尉趙萌，後軍校尉鮑信，中軍校尉袁紹，一行人眾，數百人馬，接著車駕，君臣皆哭。先使人將段珪首級往京師號令。另換好馬與帝及陳留王騎坐，簇帝還京。先是洛陽小兒謠曰：「帝非帝，王非王，千乘萬騎走北邙。」至此果應其讖。
paragraphs.prose: Now Min Gong overtook and seized Duan Gui, and asked where the Son of Heaven was. Gui said that he had been lost from him on the way, and he did not know where. Min Gong then slew Duan Gui, hung his head from his horse's neck, and divided his troops to scatter abroad and search. He himself rode alone along the road in pursuit. By chance he came to Cui Yi's manor; Yi, seeing the head, asked him, and Gong told the matter in full. Cui Yi led Gong in to see the Emperor; lord and minister wept aloud. Gong said, "The state cannot be without a sovereign for a single day; we beg Your Majesty to return to the capital." On Cui Yi's manor there was only one lean horse, and it was made ready for the Emperor to ride. Min Gong and the Prince of Chenliu shared one horse together. They had not gone three li from the manor when the Minister of the Masses Wang Yun, the Grand Commandant Yang Biao, the Colonel of the Left Army Chunyu Qiong, the Colonel of the Right Army Zhao Meng, the Colonel of the Rear Army Bao Xin, the Colonel of the Central Army Yuan Shao — a company of several hundred men and horse — met the imperial carriage, and lord and ministers all wept. They first sent a man bearing Duan Gui's head to the capital, that the head might be displayed. Then good horses were exchanged for the Emperor and the Prince of Chenliu to ride, and they escorted the Emperor back to the capital. Earlier, the children of Luoyang had sung a rhyme: "An Emperor not an Emperor, a prince not a prince — a thousand chariots and ten thousand horsemen run to Beimang." Now indeed the prophecy was fulfilled.
paragraphs.rhyme:
Min Gong came up on [Gui](char-duan-gui), and seiz'd his rein:
"Where is the Emp'ror?" [Gui](char-duan-gui): "Lost on the plain
We parted; he is gone." Gong slew [Gui](char-duan-gui), hung
The head from horse-neck; sent his troops along
To scour the country; he himself rode on,
And chanced by Cui Yi's manor ere long.
Yi saw the head, and Gong the matter told;
He led him to the Emp'ror, where tears roll'd.
Said Gong: "No state may lack its king one day;
Pray, Sire, return to court without delay."
Cui Yi had but a lean horse: Emp'ror rode;
The [Prince](char-prince-xie) and Gong, on one horse, shar'd the road.
Three li scarce travel'd from Cui Yi's domain,
They met an escort, hundred horse in train,
[Wang Yun](char-wang-yun), Yang Biao, with the Colonels four:
Chunyu, Zhao Meng, [Bao Xin](char-bao-xin), [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) — they bore
Some hundred horse, escorting in their grief;
And met the carriage, weeping with relief.
[Gui](char-duan-gui)'s head was sent before to [Luoyang](loc-luoyang)'s gate;
Fresh steeds for Emp'ror, [Prince](char-prince-xie), were chang'd in state.
And so escorted, they to capital came,
Where Luoyang children once had sung the same:
"Emp'ror not Emp'ror; prince not prince — by night,
A thousand cars, ten thousand horse take flight
To Beimang." This prophecy held right.

paragraphs.original: 車駕行不到數里，忽見旌旗蔽日，塵土遮天，一枝人馬到來。百官失色，帝亦大驚。袁紹驟馬出問何人。繡旗影裏，一將飛出，厲聲問：「天子何在？」帝戰慄不能言。陳留王勒馬向前，叱曰：「來者何人？」卓曰：「西涼刺史董卓也。」陳留王曰：「汝來保駕耶？汝來劫駕耶？」卓應曰：「特來保駕。」陳留王曰：「既來保駕，天子在此，何不下馬？」卓大驚，慌忙下馬，拜於道左。陳留王以言撫慰董卓，自初至終，並無失語。卓暗奇之，已懷廢立之意。
paragraphs.prose: The carriage had not gone many li, when suddenly they saw banners that hid the sun and dust that covered the sky, and a force of men and horse came up. The hundred officials lost their color, and the Emperor too was greatly startled. Yuan Shao galloped his horse forth and asked who was there. From the shadow of an embroidered banner, a general came flying forth, and with a stern voice asked, "Where is the Son of Heaven?" The Emperor trembled and could not speak. The Prince of Chenliu reined his horse forward and rebuked, "Who is it that comes here?" Zhuo answered, "I am Dong Zhuo, Inspector of Xiliang." The Prince of Chenliu said, "Have you come to protect the imperial carriage? Or to seize it?" Zhuo answered, "I come on purpose to protect it." The Prince of Chenliu said, "If you come to protect, the Son of Heaven is here — why do you not dismount?" Zhuo was greatly alarmed, hastily dismounted, and bowed at the left of the road. The Prince of Chenliu addressed him with soothing words; from beginning to end, he made not one slip of speech. Zhuo secretly marvelled at him, and even then began to nourish a design to depose and to install.
paragraphs.rhyme:
The carriage scarce some li had gone, when high
Came banners hiding sun, and dust the sky,
A force of men and horse came up the way;
The hundred lords grew pale, in quick dismay.
[Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) spurr'd forth: "Who comes? Declare to all!"
Beneath the broider'd flag, a chief did call,
With stern voice loud: "Where is the Heaven-Son?"
The Emp'ror trembl'd — answer he had none.
The [Prince of Chenliu](char-prince-xie) rein'd his horse and bold
Cry'd out: "Who art thou? Speak, and let thy name unfold!"
"[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) am I, Inspector of [Liang](loc-liang-province)'s land."
The [Prince](char-prince-xie): "Com'st thou to guard, or to demand
And seize?" [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo): "Sir, on purpose to defend
I came." The [Prince](char-prince-xie): "Then dost not thou descend
Before the King? He sits within this place!"
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), fearful, slid from horse, with hurried face,
And at the roadside bow'd. With soothing tone
The [Prince](char-prince-xie) spake on; no slip his speech did own.
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) marvell'd at the [Prince](char-prince-xie)'s wit so deep;
And from that hour, in heart, he 'gan to keep
A thought to depose king, exalt the [Prince](char-prince-xie)
Upon the throne — such purpose stirred within.

paragraphs.original: 是日還宮，見何太后，俱各痛哭。檢點宮中，不見了傳國玉璽。董卓屯兵城外，每日帶鐵甲馬軍入城，橫行街市，百姓惶惶不安。卓出入宮庭，略無忌憚。後軍校尉鮑信，來見袁紹，言董卓必有異心，可速除之。紹曰：「朝廷新定，未可輕動。」鮑信見王允，亦言其事。允曰：「且容商議。」信自引本部軍兵，投泰山去了。
paragraphs.prose: That day they returned to the palace, and saw Empress Dowager He, and all wept bitterly. They examined the palace, and found that the Hereditary Seal of State was missing. Dong Zhuo encamped his troops outside the city, and every day brought iron-armored cavalry within the gates, who passed through the streets and markets at will, until the common people were dismayed and ill at ease. Zhuo passed in and out of the palace courts without the smallest scruple. The Colonel of the Rear Army Bao Xin came to see Yuan Shao, and said that Dong Zhuo surely harbored a different intent, and must be removed without delay. Shao said, "The court is but newly settled; one may not act in haste." Bao Xin went to see Wang Yun, and told him the same. Yun said, "Let it be considered for a while." Xin then led his own troops away, and went off to Mount Tai.
paragraphs.rhyme:
That day, the Emp'ror to the palace came;
[Empress](char-empress-he) and all wept loud, in tears the same.
They search'd the inner courts, and missing found
The [Imperial Seal](misc-imperial-seal): no trace upon the ground.
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) encamp'd his troops without the wall;
Each day, his iron-clad horse he led withal
Within the streets, where market-throngs were prest;
Folk look'd upon his march with sore unrest.
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) enter'd palace, came and went at will,
With not a scruple, free of fear or ill.
Then [Bao Xin](char-bao-xin), Col'nel of the Rear, address'd
To [Shao](char-yuan-shao): "[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) bears treason in his breast;
We must remove him quickly — ere his sway."
Said [Shao](char-yuan-shao): "The court is settled but to-day,
We may not move in haste." To [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) then
Bao went; Yun said: "Let counsel come again."
[Bao Xin](char-bao-xin), his troops drew off — to Mount Tai went,
And left the courtly stage, in discontent.

paragraphs.original: 董卓招誘何進兄弟部下之兵，盡歸掌握。私謂李儒曰：「吾欲廢帝立陳留王，何如？」李儒曰：「今朝廷無主，不就此時行事，遲則有變矣。來日於溫明園中，召集百官，諭以廢立；有不從者斬之，則威權之行，正在今日。」
paragraphs.prose: Dong Zhuo gathered to himself the troops that had been under the command of He Jin and his brother, and all came into his hand. He spoke privately to Li Ru, "I would depose the Emperor and set up the Prince of Chenliu — what sayest thou?" Li Ru said, "Now the court has no master; if not at this hour, then later there shall come a change. Tomorrow, in the Wenming Garden, gather all the hundred officials, and there announce the deposition and installation; those who consent not, slay them — and the exercise of authority shall begin this very day."
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) received [He Jin](char-he-jin)'s whole brothers' troops,
And gather'd all their bands into his groups.
To [Li Ru](char-li-ru), privately, he spake: "I'd will
Depose the king, set [Chenliu's Prince](char-prince-xie) to fill
The throne. What thinkest thou?" [Li Ru](char-li-ru): "The state
Hath now no master; if we waste, too late
Shall come the change. Tomorrow, gather all
The hundred lords in Wenming Garden hall;
Declare the change of throne; whoe'er deny,
Shall by the sword that very moment die.
And so thy reign and power shall hold sway:
The exercise begins this very day."

paragraphs.original: 卓喜。次日大排筵會，遍請公卿。公卿皆懼董卓，誰敢不到？卓待百官到了，然後徐徐到園門下馬，帶劍入席。酒行數巡，卓教停酒止樂，乃厲聲曰：「吾有一言，眾官靜聽。」眾官側耳。卓曰：「天子為萬民之主，無威儀不可以奉宗廟社稷。今上懦弱，不若陳留王聰明好學，可承大位。吾欲廢帝，立陳留王，諸大臣以為何如？」誅官聽罷，不敢出聲。座上一人推案直出，立於筵前，大呼：「不可！不可！汝是何人，敢發大語？天子乃先帝嫡子，初無過失，何得妄議廢立？汝欲為篡逆耶？」卓視之，乃荊州刺史丁原也。卓怒叱曰：「順我者生，逆我者死！」遂掣佩劍欲斬丁原。
paragraphs.prose: Dong Zhuo was pleased. The next day he set out a grand banquet, and summoned all the high officials. The high officials all feared Dong Zhuo — who dared not come? When the hundred officials had assembled, Zhuo at length came to the garden gate, dismounted, and entered with sword in hand. After the wine had gone several rounds, Zhuo ordered the wine and music to be stopped, and with a stern voice said, 'I have a word — let all the officials listen in silence.' The officials lent their ears. Zhuo said, 'The Son of Heaven is lord of the myriad people; without majesty he cannot serve the ancestral temples and the altars of the state. The present sovereign is weak and faint, and is not equal to the Prince of Chenliu, who is intelligent and fond of learning, and may inherit the great throne. I would depose the Emperor and set up the Prince of Chenliu — what say the great ministers?' The officials, having heard, dared not speak a word. From his seat, one man pushed back his table and came forth, stood before the feast, and cried aloud, 'It must not be! It must not be! Who art thou, that thou darest send forth such great words? The Son of Heaven is the lawful son of the late Emperor, and from his outset hath no fault; how then mayest thou recklessly discuss deposition and installation? Wouldst thou be a usurper and traitor?' Zhuo looked, and it was the Inspector of Jingzhou Ding Yuan. Zhuo, in fury, rebuked him, saying, 'Who follows me, lives; who defies me, dies!' And he drew his sword to slay Ding Yuan.
paragraphs.rhyme:
Then [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), well-pleas'd, the morrow held a fete,
And bade the hundred lords; none dared be late.
For fear of [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), the lords made hast'ning way;
When all had come, then [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), in slow array,
Came to the garden's gate, dismounted there,
And sword in hand, took up the feaster's chair.
The wine some rounds had pass'd; he bade it cease,
And music too; the hall now hush'd to peace,
He sternly spake: "Hear, lords — one word I bear;
Let all attend in silence." Lent they ear.
"The Heaven-Son, who lord of all men reigns,
Must bear high majesty; without those strains,
He cannot duly serve th'ancestral shrine,
Nor altars of the state, of royal line.
Our King is faint; not [Chenliu](char-prince-xie)'s match in wit,
Whose love of books makes him for ruling fit.
I'd take him down, the [Prince](char-prince-xie) to crown instead:
What say my lords?" None spake — they sat in dread.
Then one in anger push'd his board aside,
Stood forth before the feast, and loud he cri'd:
"It shall not be! Not so! Who art thou, then,
To dare such words before the hundred men?
The Heaven-Son, the late king's lawful son,
Hath fault'd nothing since his reign begun;
How dar'st thou wantonly his throne debate?
Wouldst thou usurp, and play the traitor's state?"
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) look'd: 'twas [Ding Yuan](char-ding-yuan), of [Jingzhou](loc-jing-province)'s land;
With wrath he bark'd this threat, with sword at hand:
"Who follows me shall live; who dares deny,
Beneath this very blade he straight shall die!"
He drew his blade — to lay [Ding Yuan](char-ding-yuan) in dust,
With wrath so hot that none could stay his thrust.

paragraphs.original: 時李儒見丁原背後一人，生得器字軒昂，威風凜凜，手執方天畫戟，怒目而視。李儒急進曰：「今日飲宴之處，不可談國政；來日向都堂公論未遲。」眾人皆勸丁原上馬而去。卓問百官曰：「吾所言，合公道否？」盧植曰：「明公差矣：昔太甲不明，伊尹放之於桐宮。昌邑王登位方二十七日，造惡三千餘條，故霍光告太廟而廢之。今上雖幼，聰明仁智，並無分毫過失。公乃外郡刺史，素未參與國政，又無伊、霍之大才，何可強主廢立之事？聖人云『有伊尹之志則可，無伊尹之志則篡也。』」卓大怒，拔劍向前欲殺植。議郎彭伯諫曰：「盧尚書海內人望，今先害之，恐天下震怖。」卓乃止。司徒王允曰：「廢立之事，不可酒後相商，另日再議。」於是百官皆散。卓按劍立於園門，忽見一人躍馬持戟，於園門外往來馳驟。卓問李儒：「此何人也？」儒曰：「此丁原義兄：姓呂，名布，字奉先者也。主公且須避之。」卓乃入園潛避。
paragraphs.prose: At that moment Li Ru saw a man behind Ding Yuan — of imposing stature and awe-inspiring presence, holding a Square-Heaven Painted Halberd, glaring with angry eyes. Li Ru hastily came forward and said, 'A place of feasting and wine is no fit place to discuss the affairs of state; tomorrow, in the council hall, public debate will not be too late.' All urged Ding Yuan to mount and depart. Zhuo asked the hundred officials, 'Do my words accord with public right?' Lu Zhi said, 'Your Lordship is mistaken. Of old, Tai Jia was without understanding, and Yi Yin banished him to the Palace of Tong. The King of Changyi had ascended the throne but seven and twenty days, and had committed more than three thousand evils — therefore Huo Guang reported it to the ancestral temple, and deposed him. The present sovereign, though young, is intelligent, benevolent, and wise, and has not the smallest fault. You, sir, are but the Inspector of an outer commandery; you have never had part in the government of the state, nor have you the great gifts of a Yi Yin or a Huo Guang — how can you presume to lead the matter of deposition and installation? The Sage has said: "He who hath Yi Yin's intent, may do it; he who hath not Yi Yin's intent, doth usurp."' Zhuo, in great wrath, drew his sword and came forward to kill Lu Zhi. The Counsellor Peng Bo remonstrated, saying, 'Master Secretary Lu is one whom the whole realm holds in high esteem; should you harm him first, the empire would tremble in terror.' Zhuo desisted. The Minister of the Masses Wang Yun said, 'The matter of deposition and installation cannot be settled over wine; let it be debated again on another day.' Thereupon all the officials dispersed. Zhuo, with hand on sword, stood at the garden gate, when suddenly he saw a man on a leaping horse, halberd in hand, galloping to and fro outside the gate. Zhuo asked Li Ru, 'Who is that?' Ru said, 'That is Ding Yuan's foster son — surname Lü, name Bu, courtesy Fengxian. Your Lordship had best avoid him for now.' Zhuo then went into the garden to hide.
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Li Ru](char-li-ru) beheld a man at [Ding Yuan](char-ding-yuan)'s back,
Of stately mien, with martial force full-packed;
He bore a Square-of-Heav'n Halberd in might,
And glar'd with wrathful eyes in [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s full sight.
[Li Ru](char-li-ru) came forth in haste: "This day of cheer
Is no fit place for state-affairs to clear;
Tomorrow, in the council-hall, debate
May yet proceed — the moment is not late."
The lords urg'd [Ding Yuan](char-ding-yuan) to depart with speed;
He mounted, rode away. [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) took the lead:
"What I have said, doth public truth allow?"
[Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi) reply'd: "Your Lordship errs e'en now.
Of old, Tai Jia, dim-mind'd, knew no light;
Yi Yin to Tong's Palace cast him from his right.
King Changyi reign'd but sev'n-and-twenty days,
With more than thrice a thousand sinful ways;
So Huo Guang at the temple told the deed,
And from the throne the king was forc'd to cede.
Our King, though young, is bright, benign, and wise;
No fault in him is found by mortal eyes.
Thou art but Inspector of an outer state,
Hast had no share in council's high debate,
Nor hast thou Yi Yin's nor Huo Guang's high gift —
How dar'st thou kingly station strive to shift?
The Sage hath said: 'With Yi Yin's mind in view,
'Tis right; without it, treason doth ensue.'"
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), mad with rage, his sword drew forth to slay;
Then Counsel'lor Peng Bo stood athwart his way:
"Master Lu, the realm's renown'd and lov'd by all;
To slay him first, the empire's heart will fall."
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) stay'd his hand. The Minister, [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun),
Then spake: "Such weighty change is not to run
Through wine; another day shall this debate
Be settled." So the hundred lords sought the gate.
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), sword in hand, beside the garden door
Stood, when a horseman, halberd-arm'd, before
The gateway wheel'd, and gallop'd to and fro.
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) ask'd [Li Ru](char-li-ru): "What man rides yon? Pray show."
"'Tis [Ding Yuan](char-ding-yuan)'s foster son," [Ru](char-li-ru) reply'd:
"Surnamed [Lü](char-lu-bu), named [Bu](char-lu-bu), [Fengxian](char-lu-bu) styled beside.
My Lord, for now avoid his fearsome might."
Then [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) retir'd, to shun the warrior's sight.

paragraphs.original: 次日，人報丁原引軍城外搦戰。卓怒，引軍同李儒出迎。兩陣對圓，只見呂布頂束髮金冠，披百花戰袍，擐唐猊鎧甲，繫獅蠻寶帶，縱馬挺戟，隨丁建陽出到陣前。建陽指卓罵曰：「國家不幸，閹官弄權，以致萬民塗炭。爾無尺寸之功，焉敢妄言廢立，欲亂朝廷？」
paragraphs.prose: The next day, a messenger reported that Ding Yuan was leading his army outside the city to challenge battle. Dong Zhuo, in anger, led out his troops with Li Ru to meet him. The two armies drew up face to face; and there appeared Lü Bu, wearing a golden hair-binding crown, clad in a hundred-flower battle-robe, in mail of the Tang lion, with a lion-man jeweled belt at his waist, urging his horse and brandishing his halberd, following Ding Jianyang out to the front of his lines. Jianyang pointed at Zhuo and reviled him, saying: 'The state is in misfortune; eunuch officers have laid hold of power, that the myriad people have come to mire and ash. Thou hast not a chi or cun of merit — how darest thou wantonly speak of deposition and installation, and seek to throw the court into disorder?'
paragraphs.rhyme:
The morrow's news: "[Ding Yuan](char-ding-yuan), without the wall,
Now leads his men, and challenge sounds his call."
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), fierce with wrath, with [Li Ru](char-li-ru) rode amain,
To meet him in the field. The level plain
Saw two array'd hosts. Then rode forth [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu),
With golden hair-binding crown of stately hue,
A robe of hundred-flowers, warlike-bright,
Tang-lion mail, that gleam'd on him in light,
A jewel'd lion-belt about his waist;
With urging horse, his halberd shook in haste,
With [Ding Jianyang](char-ding-yuan) rode [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) by his side;
Then [Ding](char-ding-yuan) at [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) with pointing finger cri'd:
"The state is luckless; eunuch hands have play'd
With pow'r, till myriad folk in ash are laid.
Thou hast no merit, chi nor cun to show:
Dar'st thou depose the king, the court o'erthrow?"

paragraphs.original: 董卓未及回言，呂布飛馬直殺過來。董卓慌走，建陽率軍掩殺。卓兵大敗，退三十餘里下寨，聚眾商議。卓曰：「吾觀呂布非常人也。吾若得此人，何慮天下哉？」帳前一人出曰：「主公勿憂：某與呂布同鄉，知其勇而無謀，見利忘義。某憑三寸不爛之舌，說呂布拱手來降，可乎？」
paragraphs.prose: Dong Zhuo had not yet had time to answer when Lü Bu, on his flying horse, came hurtling straight forward to slay him. Dong Zhuo fled in panic, and Jianyang, leading his troops, pressed in. Zhuo's army was greatly defeated, and fell back more than thirty li to encamp, where they gathered in council. Zhuo said: 'I see that Lü Bu is no common man. If I could win him to my side, what concern should I have for the empire?' From before the tent one stepped forth and said: 'Let Your Lordship not be troubled: I am Lü Bu's fellow-countryman, and know him to be brave but unstrategic, and one who forgets right at the sight of gain. By the strength of my three-cun unrotted tongue, I will persuade Lü Bu to come over with cupped hands in submission. May it be done?'
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s answer scarce had risen on his tongue,
When [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu)'s flying horse upon him sprung;
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) fled in fear; [Jianyang](char-ding-yuan) his troops led on,
And press'd the tyrant. [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s whole host was gone,
Defeated, thirty li he fell behind,
And pitch'd his camp, and call'd his lords to mind:
Said [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo): "I see [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu)'s no common man:
Could I but win him, who'd resist my plan
Throughout the realm?" Then one before the tent
Stepp'd forth and spake: "Be cheer'd; thy fears relent:
The same home-village [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) I have known;
His courage great, yet plans he hath not shown:
He sees a gain, and duty's bond resigns.
With tongue of three cun, deft in winning lines,
[Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) shall come, hands-cupp'd, to join thy band:
My Lord, may I assay, by thy command?"

paragraphs.original: 卓大喜，觀其人，乃虎賁中郎李肅也。卓曰：「汝將何以說之？」肅曰：「某聞主公有名馬一匹，號曰『赤兔』，日行千里。須得此馬，再用金珠，以利結其心。某更進說詞，呂布必反丁原，來投主公矣。」卓問李儒曰：「此言可乎？」儒曰：「主公欲取天下，何惜一馬？」卓欣然與之，更與黃金一千兩、明珠數十顆、玉帶一條。
paragraphs.prose: Zhuo, greatly pleased, looked at the man; it was the General of the Tiger Guards, Li Su. Zhuo said: 'How wilt thou win him over?' Su said: 'I hear that Your Lordship has a famous horse, named Red Hare, that goes a thousand li in a day. We must have this horse, and join to it gold and pearls, to bind his heart through gain. With my added words of persuasion, Lü Bu shall surely turn against Ding Yuan and come over to Your Lordship.' Zhuo asked Li Ru, 'Will this proposal serve?' Ru said: 'If Your Lordship would take the empire, why begrudge a single horse?' Zhuo readily granted it, and added a thousand liang of gold, several dozen bright pearls, and one jade belt.
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), greatly pleas'd, beheld the man, and knew
'Twas [Li Su](char-li-su), the Tiger Guards' General true.
"How wilt thou speak with him?" [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) ask'd in turn.
[Su](char-li-su): "Thou hast, my Lord, a horse of swift concern,
[Red Hare](misc-red-hare) by name, that runs a thousand li
Each day; with horse, with gold and pearls in fee,
His heart, through gain, shall yield without delay;
My speech beside, his change is on the way:
[Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) shall turn from [Ding Yuan](char-ding-yuan)'s banner sure,
And come, hands-cupp'd, to thy command secure."
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) ask'd [Li Ru](char-li-ru): "Doth this thy counsel hold?"
[Ru](char-li-ru): "Wouldst thou win the realm, and yet withhold
A single horse?" [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) gladly gave the steed;
And added gifts to make the matter speed:
Bright gold, a thousand liang; bright pearls, by tens;
And one jade-belt, that summ'd the giver's ends.

paragraphs.original: 李肅齎了禮物，投呂布寨來。伏路軍人圍住。肅曰：「可速報呂將軍，有故人來見。」軍人報知，布命入見。肅見布曰：「賢弟別來無恙！」布揖曰：「久不相見，今居何處？」肅曰：「見任虎賁中郎將之職。聞賢弟匡扶社稷，不勝之喜。有良馬一匹，日行千里，渡水登山，如履平地，名曰『赤兔』：特獻與賢弟，以助虎威。」布便令牽過來看。果然那馬渾身上下，火炭般赤，無半根雜毛；從頭至尾，長一丈；從蹄至項，高八尺；嘶喊咆哮，有騰空入海之狀。後人有詩單道赤兔馬曰：　　奔騰千里蕩塵埃，渡水登山紫霧開。掣斷絲韁搖玉轡，火龍飛下九天來。
paragraphs.prose: Li Su, bearing the gifts, set out for Lü Bu's camp. The soldiers on patrol encircled him. Su said, 'Quickly inform General Lü — an old friend has come to see him.' The soldiers reported it, and Bu bade him be brought in. Su, on seeing Bu, said, 'My worthy younger brother — I trust you have been well since we parted!' Bu, with a salute, said, 'Long have we been apart; where are you now stationed?' Su said, 'I now hold the office of General of the Tiger Guards. Hearing that my worthy younger brother is sustaining the altars of state, I am beyond measure pleased. I have one fine horse — he goes a thousand li in a day; he crosses waters and climbs mountains as though treading level ground; his name is "Red Hare." This I present in particular to my worthy younger brother, to aid your tiger-might.' Bu at once bade them lead the horse forth for him to see. Indeed, the horse from head to foot was red as glowing coal — not a single hair of any other color; from head to tail he was one zhang in length, from hoof to neck eight chi in height; his neighing and roaring had the air of one who would mount the heavens and plunge into the seas. A later poet wrote a piece in praise of Red Hare alone, saying: 'Bounding a thousand li, he sweeps the dust away; / Crossing waters, climbing mountains, the purple mists divide. / He snaps the silken rein and shakes the jade bridle; / A fire-dragon descended from the Ninth Heaven.'
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Li Su](char-li-su), with gifts, to [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu)'s camp drew near;
The roadside guards encircled, sword and spear.
Said [Su](char-li-su): 'Pray swift to Gen'ral [Lü](char-lu-bu) declare
That an old friend awaits before him there.'
The men announc'd; [Bu](char-lu-bu) had the guest brought through.
Said [Su](char-li-su): 'Dear brother, well I trust with you?'
[Bu](char-lu-bu) bow'd: 'Long parted, friend! What place hold'st thou?'
Said [Su](char-li-su): 'Of the Tiger Guards, General now.
Glad am I, brother, that thou prop'st the throne,
And to thy name great loyalty is known.
A horse have I, a thousand li each day;
O'er stream and crag he treads as level way;
[Red Hare](misc-red-hare) his name; my gift, dear brother — take,
And swell thy tiger-might for glory's sake.'
Then [Lü](char-lu-bu) bade bring the steed before his eye:
Like coal-fire red, no hair of other dye;
A zhang from snout to tail his length doth claim,
Eight chi from hoof to neck — a fiery frame;
With neighing roar, he seem'd the clouds to ride,
Or plunge the deeps, in proud commanding stride.
A later poet sang [Red Hare](misc-red-hare) aright,
And in these lines set forth its wondrous might:
'A thousand li he runs, and dust departs;
O'er stream and hill, the purple mist outstarts.
The silken rein he snaps, the jade bit shakes;
Down from the Heaven's Nine, a fire-dragon breaks.'

paragraphs.original: 布見了此馬，大喜，謝肅曰：「兄賜此良駒，將何以為報？」肅曰：「某為義氣而來，豈望報乎？」布置酒相待。酒酣，肅曰：「肅與賢弟少得相見；令尊卻常會來。」布曰：「兄醉矣！先父棄世多年，安得與兄相會？」肅大笑曰：「非也﹔某說今日丁刺史耳。」布惶恐曰：「某在丁建陽處，亦出於無奈。」肅曰：「賢弟有擎天駕海之才，四海孰不欽敬？功名富貴，如探囊取物，何言無奈而在人之下乎？」布曰：「恨不逢其主耳。」肅笑曰：「『良禽擇木而棲，賢臣擇主而事。』見機不早，悔之晚矣。」布曰：「兄在朝廷，觀何人為世之英雄？」肅曰：「某遍觀群臣，皆不如董卓，董卓為人敬賢禮士，賞罰分明，終成大業。」布曰：「某欲從之，恨無門路。」
paragraphs.prose: Lü Bu, on seeing the horse, was greatly pleased, and thanked Su, saying, 'My elder brother has bestowed on me this fine steed; how shall I repay you?' Su said, 'I came out of righteous feeling — how should I look for repayment?' Bu set out wine to entertain him. When the wine had risen high, Su said, 'My worthy younger brother and I have had little opportunity of meeting; your honored sire, however, often used to come to me.' Bu said, 'My elder brother is drunk! My late father departed this world many years ago; how could he meet with you?' Su laughed aloud, saying, 'Not so; I was speaking of the present Inspector Ding.' Bu, in alarm, said, 'My presence at Ding Jianyang's quarters is itself from no choice of mine.' Su said, 'My worthy younger brother, with talent to pillar the heavens and ride the seas — within the four seas, who would not look on you with reverence? Fame, rank, wealth, and honor, would be to you as reaching into a bag for what lies within; why then speak of necessity, and of being beneath another?' Bu said, 'I lament only that I have not met my true lord.' Su laughed, saying, '"A good bird chooses its tree to roost; a wise minister chooses his lord to serve." If you do not see the opportunity early, repentance will come too late.' Bu said, 'My elder brother is at court — whom do you see as the hero of the age?' Su said, 'Of all the ministers I have looked upon, none is the equal of Dong Zhuo: in his nature, Dong Zhuo reveres the worthy and honors the gentleman, his rewards and punishments are clearly distinguished, and in the end he shall accomplish a great work.' Bu said, 'I would follow him, yet I regret that I have no road thither.'
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Bu](char-lu-bu), seeing it, was glad, and thank'd his friend:
'Such steed bestow'd — how shall my thanks extend?'
[Su](char-li-su): 'I for honor's sake am hither come;
What thought of recompense should make me dumb?'
[Lü](char-lu-bu) set out wine to feast his guest with cheer;
When wine had pass'd some rounds, [Su](char-li-su) spake to ear:
'My brother, scarce have we two met of late;
Thy honor'd father, though, would oft await
A chance to come.' [Bu](char-lu-bu) cried: 'Thou must be drunk!
My father long ago to death hath sunk —
How could'st thou meet?' [Su](char-li-su) laugh'd, and made reply:
'Not so — [Inspector Ding](char-ding-yuan) I meant thereby.'
[Bu](char-lu-bu) blush'd: 'I serve at [Ding](char-ding-yuan)'s, of dire need;
No will of mine to that hath given heed.'
Said [Su](char-li-su): 'My brother — thine the strength to be
A pillar of the sky, who reins the sea.
Beneath the heavens, who would not revere?
Fame, rank, and wealth, to thee, all hover near,
As one might pluck a thing from bag at hand.
Why pleadest duress, 'neath another's stand?'
[Bu](char-lu-bu): 'I but mourn — no rightful lord I find.'
Said [Su](char-li-su), with smile: 'A truth of older mind:
"A goodly bird picks out the tree to nest;
A worthy vassal picks the lord most blest."
If thou the chance dost spy, but tarry slow,
Repentance comes too late, when chance is low.'
[Bu](char-lu-bu): 'Brother, thou at court hast wider sight,
Whom hold'st thou hero of this age's plight?'
[Su](char-li-su): 'Through all the lords my searching eyes have stray'd,
None matcheth [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), in whose being weigh'd
The honor of the worthy, scholars' grace,
With clear rewards and punishments in place.
A pillar of the realm at last he'll stand,
And great achievements shall fulfil his hand.'
[Bu](char-lu-bu): 'Him would I serve, but still no path is plain
By which I may to him admittance gain.'

paragraphs.original: 肅取金珠、玉帶列於布前。布驚曰：「何為有此？」肅令叱退左右，告布曰：「此是董公久慕大名，特令某將此奉獻。赤兔馬亦董公所贈也。」布曰：「董公如此見愛，某將何以報之？」肅曰：「如某之不才，尚為虎賁中郎將；公若到彼，貴不可言。」布曰：「恨無涓埃之功，以為進見之禮。」肅曰：「功在翻手之間，公不肯為耳。」布沈吟良久曰：「吾欲殺丁原，引軍歸董卓，何如？」肅曰：「賢弟若能如此，真莫大之功也！但事不宜遲，在於速決。」
paragraphs.prose: Su took out the gold, the pearls, and the jade belt, and arrayed them before Bu. Bu was startled and said, 'Why have you brought these?' Su had the attendants dismissed, and told Bu, 'This is because Lord Dong has long admired your great name; he expressly bade me bring you these gifts. The Red Hare horse, too, was a present from Lord Dong.' Bu said, 'Lord Dong cherishes me thus; how shall I repay him?' Su said, 'A man of my poor talents now holds the office of General of the Tiger Guards; should you come over to him, your honor would be beyond words.' Bu said, 'I regret only that I have not so much as a droplet's or a speck's worth of merit to bring as gift for the first audience.' Su said, 'The merit lies between the turning of a hand; only you are not willing to do it.' Bu pondered for a long while, and said, 'I would kill Ding Yuan and lead his troops over to Dong Zhuo. What say you?' Su said, 'If my worthy younger brother can do this, truly there is no greater merit! But the matter must not be delayed; it rests in a swift decision.'
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Su](char-li-su) set the gold and pearls and jade in row
Before [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu). [Lü](char-lu-bu) started: 'Whence this show?'
[Su](char-li-su) bade the servants forth; then he reveal'd:
'[Lord Dong](char-dong-zhuo), with admiration long conceal'd
For thy great name, hath bade me bring this freight.
The Red Hare too is [Dong](char-dong-zhuo)'s bestowal great.'
[Bu](char-lu-bu): '[Lord Dong](char-dong-zhuo) such grace upon me hath display'd,
What service from my hand may be array'd?'
[Su](char-li-su): 'I, of poor and slender gift, command
A General's rank in the Tiger Guards' band;
Shouldst thou approach him, honor past all phrase
Awaits thee, brother, in the coming days.'
[Bu](char-lu-bu): 'Yet no drop of dew, no speck of dust
Of merit have I, to present in trust
At my first audience.' [Su](char-li-su) reply'd: 'The deed
Lies in the turning of a hand at need,
Only thou'rt loath to act.' [Bu](char-lu-bu), deep in thought,
A long time pond'red, ere reply he wrought:
'I would slay [Ding Yuan](char-ding-yuan), and with all his men
Pass over to [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s banner — then,
Say, what dost thou advise?' [Su](char-li-su) cried: 'If true,
No greater merit canst thou bring to view!
But haste! The deed admits no slow delay,
In swift resolve thy fortune lies this day.'

paragraphs.original: 布與肅約於明日來降，肅別去。是夜二更時分，布提刀逕入丁原帳中。原正秉燭觀書，見布至，曰：「吾兒來有何事故？」布曰：「吾堂堂丈夫，安肯為汝子乎！」原曰：「奉先何故心變？」布向前一刀砍下丁原首級，大呼：「左右！丁原不仁，吾已殺之。肯從吾者在此，不從者自去！」軍士散其大半。
paragraphs.prose: Bu agreed with Su to come over the next day; and Su took his leave and departed. That night, about the second watch, Bu, with sword in hand, walked straight into Ding Yuan's tent. Yuan was at that moment holding a candle and reading. Seeing Bu come in, he said, 'My son — for what cause are you here?' Bu said, 'I am a fine, upright man — how should I willingly be your son?' Yuan said, 'Fengxian — wherefore is your heart changed?' Bu went forward, and with one stroke cut off Ding Yuan's head, and shouted aloud, 'Attendants! Ding Yuan was unkind; I have already slain him. Those who would follow me, remain; those who would not, depart!' More than half of the troops scattered.
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Bu](char-lu-bu) and [Li Su](char-li-su) agreed: by morrow's light,
[Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) would yield. [Su](char-li-su) parted, ere the night.
At second watch, [Bu](char-lu-bu), with sword-blade bright,
Slipt to [Ding Yuan](char-ding-yuan)'s tent in stealth of night.
[Yuan](char-ding-yuan) held a taper, reading there alone;
He saw [Bu](char-lu-bu) come, and said in father's tone:
'My son, what cause hath brought thee to my side?'
[Bu](char-lu-bu) cri'd: 'A man of stature — how abide
The name of "son" to thee?' [Yuan](char-ding-yuan): '[Fengxian](char-lu-bu), why
Hath turn'd thy heart?' [Bu](char-lu-bu) sprang, with sword on high,
And cleft [Yuan](char-ding-yuan)'s head with one keen stroke. He cry'd
With thund'rous voice: 'Ye men — to me, allied!
[Ding Yuan](char-ding-yuan) was harsh; by me hath he been slain.
Who'd follow me, here in this camp remain;
Who will not, take their leave and freely go.'
The greater half dispers'd, in scatter'd row.

paragraphs.original: 次日，布持丁原首級，往見李肅。肅遂引布見卓。卓大喜，置酒相待。卓先下拜曰：「卓今得將軍，如旱苗之得甘雨也。」布納卓坐而拜之曰：「公若不棄，布請拜為義父。」卓以金甲錦袍賜布，暢飲而散。卓自是威勢越大，自領前將軍事，封弟董旻為左將軍鄠侯，封呂布為騎都尉中郎將都亭侯。李儒勸卓早定廢立之計。卓乃於省中設宴，會集公卿，令呂布將甲士千餘，侍衛左右。
paragraphs.prose: The next day, Bu, bearing the head of Ding Yuan, went to see Li Su; and Su led him in to see Dong Zhuo. Zhuo, greatly pleased, set out wine to entertain him. Zhuo first bowed before him and said, 'My obtaining General Bu this day is as parched seedlings getting sweet rain.' Bu seated Zhuo, and bowed to him in turn, saying, 'If My Lord do not reject me, I, Bu, beg leave to bow to you as my foster father.' Zhuo bestowed on Bu a coat of golden armor and a brocade robe; they drank to their fill, and the company dispersed. Zhuo's authority and power from this grew greater still: he took to himself the office of General of the Front; enfeoffed his younger brother Dong Min as General of the Left and Marquis of Hu; and enfeoffed Lü Bu as Cavalry Commandant, General of the Household, and Marquis of Duting. Li Ru urged Zhuo to settle the deposition and installation plan early. Zhuo therefore set out a banquet in the inner palace, gathered the high officials together, and bade Lü Bu lead more than a thousand armored men, in attendance to right and left.
paragraphs.rhyme:
Next day, [Bu](char-lu-bu) bore the slain head of his lord
To [Li Su](char-li-su)'s quarter; [Su](char-li-su), by quick accord,
Brought [Bu](char-lu-bu) before [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo). [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), full of glee,
Set forth the wine, and bow'd: 'In gaining thee,
I'm as the parch'd young shoots, when rains descend
With sweetness.' [Bu](char-lu-bu) return'd the bow, to bend,
And said: 'My Lord, disdain me not, I pray,
I'd call thee foster father, from this day.'
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) gave a gold-mail coat, and brocade bright
Of robe; they drank in deep and long delight,
Then parted. [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s authority grew great
From that hour on. He took for self-estate
The General of the Front; his brother grew,
Dong Min — to General of the Left, anew;
And Marquis of Hu by title was confirm'd.
[Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) was Cavalry Commandant term'd,
House-General, and Marquis of Duting too,
Three offices in one bestowal due.
[Li Ru](char-li-ru) then urg'd: 'My Lord, no more delay,
Set the throne's change, without a moment's stay.'
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) therefore set, within the palace hall,
A banquet, and convok'd the lords of all.
[Lü Bu](char-lu-bu), with thousand arm'd men, by command,
Stood guard around the feast, on either hand.

paragraphs.original: 是日，太傳袁隗與百官皆到。酒行數巡，卓拔劍曰：「今上闇弱，不可以奉宗廟；吾將依伊尹、霍光故事，廢帝為弘農王，立陳留王皇帝。有不從者斬！」群臣惶怖莫敢對。中軍校尉袁紹挺身出曰：「今上即位未幾，並無失德；汝欲廢嫡立庶，非反而何？」卓怒曰：「天下事在我！我今為之，誰敢不從？汝視我之劍不利否？」袁紹亦拔劍曰：「汝劍利，吾劍未嘗不利！」兩個在筵上對敵。正是：　　丁原仗義身先喪，袁紹爭鋒勢又危。畢竟袁紹性命如何，且聽下文分解。
paragraphs.prose: That day, the Grand Tutor Yuan Wei and all the officials came. After the wine had passed several rounds, Zhuo drew his sword and said, 'The present Emperor is dim and weak, and cannot serve the ancestral temple. I will follow the precedents of Yi Yin and Huo Guang: I shall depose the Emperor and make him Prince of Hongnong, and set up the Prince of Chenliu as Emperor. Whoever does not comply shall be slain!' The whole assembly was filled with terror, and none dared answer. The Colonel of the Central Army Yuan Shao stood forth and said, 'The present Emperor has but newly ascended, and is in no respect lacking in virtue. You would depose the lawful heir and install the secondary — if this is not rebellion, what is it?' Zhuo, in anger, said, 'The affairs of the empire lie in my hand! When I do this today, who dares not follow? Behold my sword — is it not sharp?' Yuan Shao likewise drew his sword and said, 'Your sword is sharp; my sword has never been less than sharp!' And the two of them confronted each other in adversary at the banquet table. As the verse runs: 'Ding Yuan stood by righteousness, and his life was the first to fall; / Yuan Shao now contends in arms, and his peril rises in turn.' Whether Yuan Shao keeps his life or loses it, listen to the next chapter for the answer.
paragraphs.rhyme:
That day [Yuan Wei](char-yuan-wei), the Grand-Tutor renown'd,
With all the hundred lords, at feast was found.
As wine had circled, [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) unsheath'd his sword;
And spake, his stern address to every lord:
'The King is dim and weak, unfit to bear
The duties of the altars' sacred care.
I'll tread the path of Yi Yin, Huo Guang's name:
Depose the King, to Hongnong's princely fame;
Set [Chenliu's Prince](char-prince-xie) upon the throne of state;
Whoso defies — the sword be on his pate!'
The hundred lords sat frozen, dar'd not stir;
[Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao), of Central host, sprang forth to spur
A protest: 'Newly mounted to his place,
Our King — no fault hath stain'd his royal grace.
Wouldst thou the lawful king depose, and crown
The lesser-born? What's this but treason known?'
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), in great wrath, exclaim'd: 'The empire's might
Lies in my hand! Who dares to thwart my right?
Behold this sword — is it not keen and sure?'
[Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) drew forth his blade, with answer pure:
'Thy sword is keen — but mine no less the same!'
The banquet table was their field of flame.
Hereon a poet's pen this scene doth frame:
'[Ding Yuan](char-ding-yuan) stood by right — his life was first to fall;
[Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) now strives — his peril hears its call.'
Whether [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) live or lose his breath,
Next chapter shall resolve of life or death.
